questions.question: Which of the following option is NOT true for unorganised sector?

options.text: There is a provision for paid leaves
Largely outside the control of government

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**There is a provision for paid leaves**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The unorganised sector refers to employment that is not registered under the government and lacks standardised rules and regulations.
 
• In the unorganised sector, workers generally do not receive paid leaves, as employers often do not provide this benefit due to the informal nature of employment.
 
• Workers in this sector face irregular and insecure employment conditions, which often do not include basic social security measures like health insurance or paid leave.
 
• The absence of paid leave provisions is a key characteristic distinguishing the unorganised sector from organised employment.
 
• The unorganised sector is largely outside the purview of government regulations, making it difficult to enforce labour laws such as paid leave benefits for workers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Frictional unemployment:**

 
 
• This is the temporary unemployment of workers who are in between jobs or are looking for their first job. It is a natural part of the job market as people switch careers or re-enter the workforce.
 
 
 
• **Structural unemployment:**
 
 
• This occurs when there is a mismatch between the skills workers have and the skills employers need. It can also happen when an industry declines, or jobs move to other regions or countries.
 
 
 
• **Cyclical unemployment:**
 
 
• This type of unemployment is directly related to the business cycle. It happens during a recession or economic downturn when demand for goods and services falls, leading companies to lay off workers.

questions.question: Which organisation formulates Fiscal Policy in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ministry of Finance**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Ministry of Finance** is responsible for formulating and overseeing the implementation of India's fiscal policy, including taxation, government spending, and borrowing.
 
• Fiscal policy in India is designed to promote economic stability, ensure equitable distribution of wealth, and achieve sustainable growth.
 
• The Ministry of Finance comprises several departments, such as the **Department of Economic Affairs**, **Department of Revenue**, and **Department of Expenditure**, which play a key role in fiscal policy formulation.
 
• It coordinates with other ministries and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to align fiscal and monetary policies for the overall economic development of the country.
 
• The annual **Union Budget**, a major tool of fiscal policy, is prepared and presented by the Ministry of Finance in the Parliament, outlining government revenues and expenditures for the upcoming financial year.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **NITI Aayog**

 
 
• NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) is the premier policy think tank of the Government of India, established in 2015 to replace the Planning Commission.
 
• Its primary role is to provide strategic and technical advice to the central and state governments on matters of policy and economic development.
 
• Unlike the Ministry of Finance, NITI Aayog does not formulate fiscal policy but focuses on long-term development strategies and fostering cooperative federalism.
 
 
 
• **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**
 
 
• The RBI is the central bank of India, responsible for formulating and implementing **monetary policy** to regulate the supply of money and credit in the economy.
 
• It manages inflation, stabilizes the currency, and ensures the smooth functioning of the banking system, but it does not oversee fiscal policy.
 
• The RBI and the Ministry of Finance often collaborate to align monetary and fiscal policies for sustainable economic growth.
 
 
 
• **State Bank of India (SBI)**
 
 
• The SBI is the largest public sector bank in India, providing banking and financial services to individuals, businesses, and governments.
 
• It plays no direct role in fiscal or monetary policymaking but implements government schemes and policies through its vast network of branches.

questions.question: Which among the following is NOT a function of Reserve Bank of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Accepting deposits from customers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) does not perform the function of accepting deposits from customers as it is not a commercial bank.
 
• RBI acts as the central bank of India and primarily focuses on regulating the banking sector and maintaining monetary stability in the economy.
 
• Commercial banks, cooperative banks, and other financial institutions are responsible for accepting deposits from the public and providing banking services.
 
• RBI’s primary functions include monetary policy formulation, currency issuance, regulation and supervision of banks, foreign exchange management, and acting as a banker to the government.
 
• Accepting deposits is not aligned with RBI’s role as a regulator and policymaker; this function is delegated to other banking entities under RBI’s supervision.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Monetary Management:**

 
 
• RBI formulates and implements monetary policy to control inflation, stabilize the currency, and foster economic growth.
 
• The primary tools used include the repo rate, reverse repo rate, cash reserve ratio (CRR), statutory liquidity ratio (SLR), and open market operations.
 
• RBI ensures adequate liquidity in the economy while maintaining price stability.
 
 
 
• **Government Debt Management:**
 
 
• RBI acts as a banker to the government and manages its borrowing program through the issuance of government securities.
 
• It facilitates the auction of treasury bills and bonds, ensures smooth functioning of the government debt market, and prevents excessive borrowing costs.
 
• RBI also advises the government on fiscal policy and debt sustainability.
 
 
 
• **Foreign Exchange Management:**
 
 
• RBI manages India’s foreign exchange reserves and ensures stability in the exchange rate of the Indian Rupee.
 
• It regulates foreign exchange transactions under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999.
 
• RBI intervenes in the foreign exchange market to curb volatility and maintain the competitiveness of Indian exports.

questions.question: In which year Economic liberalisation took place in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1991**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Economic liberalisation in India was initiated in **1991** under the leadership of the then Prime Minister, **P. V. Narasimha Rao**, with Dr. Manmohan Singh as the Finance Minister.
 
• The reforms were undertaken to address a severe **balance of payments crisis** that India was facing at the time.
 
• The liberalisation package included **reducing import tariffs, deregulating markets, reducing the role of the government in business, and opening up the economy to foreign investment**.
 
• The **New Economic Policy (NEP)** of 1991 focused on three key areas: **liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation (LPG)**.
 
• These reforms marked a paradigm shift in India's economic policies, leading to rapid economic growth and integration into the global economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key Benefits of Economic Libralisation:**

 
 
• **Higher Economic Growth:** Reduced restrictions foster efficiency and productivity, leading to faster GDP growth.
 
• **Increased Foreign Investment:** Opens economies to foreign capital, technology, and management skills.
 
• **More Choices & Lower Prices:** Competition and reduced tariffs mean wider variety of goods and services, often at lower costs for consumers.
 
• **Innovation & Efficiency:** Competition pushes businesses to upgrade technology and management practices.
 
• **Job Creation: **Growth in sectors like IT, manufacturing, and services creates new employment opportunities.
 
• **Global Integration:** Connects countries to global supply chains and international trade networks.

questions.question: Territory which is under the immediate political control of another state is called as_______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Colony**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A colony refers to a territory that is under the immediate political control of another state, often referred to as the colonizing power.
 
• Colonies are typically established through conquest, settlement, or annexation by the colonizing nation.
 
• The colonizing power exercises control over the colony's political, economic, and social systems, often exploiting its resources for economic benefits.
 
• Famous examples of colonies include India under British rule, Algeria under French control, and several African nations under European powers during the colonial era.
 
• Colonialism is often criticized for its exploitative nature and its long-term effects on the cultural, economic, and political systems of the colonized territories.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Community:**

 
 
• A community is a group of people living in the same area or having common interests, values, and practices.
 
• Communities may be based on geographical location, ethnicity, religion, profession, or shared goals.
 
• Unlike colonies, communities are not under the political control of another state but rather function autonomously or within a larger governing structure.
 
 
 
• **District:**
 
 
• A district is an administrative division within a country or region, often used for local governance purposes.
 
• Districts are created to facilitate efficient administration and may include towns, villages, or cities.
 
• Unlike colonies, districts are part of the sovereign state's administrative framework and are not under external control.
 
 
 
• **Province:**
 
 
• A province is a principal administrative division within a country, typically larger than a district.
 
• Provinces often have a degree of autonomy and are governed by regional authorities under the country's overall legal system.
 
• Unlike colonies, provinces are not externally controlled and are an integral part of the sovereign state.

questions.question: In a/an ________, each adult citizen must have one vote and each vote must have one value.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Democracy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Democracy is a form of government in which power is vested in the hands of the people, either directly or through elected representatives.
 
• In a democracy, each adult citizen has the right to vote, and each vote carries equal value, ensuring fairness and equality in decision-making.
 
• Universal adult suffrage is a fundamental principle of democracy, allowing citizens above a certain age (usually 18 years) to participate in elections irrespective of their gender, race, or social status.
 
• Democratic governance promotes transparency, accountability, and the protection of individual rights, ensuring that the government serves the interests of the people.
 
• Countries like India, the United States, and Canada are examples of democracies where citizens directly or indirectly elect their representatives.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Autocracy:**

 
 
• Autocracy is a system of government in which a single individual holds absolute power and authority over the state.
 
• It often lacks democratic principles, and citizens have limited or no participation in decision-making processes.
 
• Examples of autocratic regimes include monarchies (e.g., historical absolute monarchies) and dictatorships (e.g., North Korea).
 
 
 
• **Plutocracy:**
 
 
• Plutocracy refers to a system of governance where power is concentrated in the hands of the wealthy or those with significant financial influence.
 
• This form of government often leads to policies that favor the affluent class, sidelining the interests of the general population.
 
• While not explicitly practiced as an official system, plutocratic tendencies can be observed in countries with significant wealth disparities.
 
 
 
• **Theocracy:**
 
 
• Theocracy is a form of government in which religious leaders or institutions hold political power and governance is based on religious principles.
 
• Examples include Iran, where the Supreme Leader holds both political and religious authority, and Vatican City, governed by the Pope.
 
• In a theocracy, laws and policies are often derived from religious texts or doctrines.

questions.question: Provision of Admission and Establishment of new state is given in which article of Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 2** of the Indian Constitution deals with the formation of new states and alteration of areas, boundaries, or names of existing states.
 
• The Parliament has exclusive power to create a new state or alter the boundaries of existing states through legislation.
 
• A bill for the purpose of creating or altering a state can only be introduced in Parliament with the recommendation of the President of India.
 
• The President sends the bill to the legislature of the state(s) affected by the proposed changes for their views, but their opinion is not binding on Parliament.
 
• This article ensures flexibility in managing the territorial integrity of India while addressing administrative, cultural, and political challenges.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 1**

 
 
• Article 1 defines India as a "Union of States" and specifies the territories that constitute India.
 
• It establishes the notion that India is an indestructible union composed of destructible states, meaning states can be restructured but the union remains indivisible.
 
• The territories of India include states, Union Territories, and any territories that may be acquired in the future.
 
 
 
• **Article 2**
 
 
• This article empowers Parliament to admit new territories into the Union of India and establish new states.
 
• Unlike Article 3, which deals with the reorganization of existing states, Article 2 applies to territories that are newly acquired or merged into India.
 
• Examples include the integration of Sikkim as a state under Article 2 in 1975.
 
 
 
• **Article 4**
 
 
• Article 4 specifies that laws made under Articles 2 and 3 for the admission or establishment of new states, or the alteration of areas, boundaries, or names of existing states, are not considered amendments to the Constitution under Article 368.
 
• This ensures that such laws can be passed without requiring a special amendment process.
 
• It provides the procedural framework for implementing Articles 2 and 3.

questions.question: Which was the most important Mahajanpada among the 16 known Mahajanpadas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Magadha**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Magadha** was the most important Mahajanapada among the 16 Mahajanapadas of ancient India, flourishing between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE.
 
• It was geographically located in the modern-day Bihar region, with its capital at Rajagriha (later shifted to Pataliputra).
 
• Magadha gained supremacy due to its strategic location, fertile land, iron resources, and strong administrative structure.
 
• The Magadha region was the cradle of several major dynasties, including the Haryanka, Shishunaga, Nanda, Maurya, and Gupta dynasties.
 
• It played a pivotal role in Indian history as the center of two major religions, Buddhism and Jainism, with leaders like Gautama Buddha and Mahavira spending significant time in this region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kosala**

 
 
• Kosala was another significant Mahajanapada, situated in present-day Uttar Pradesh.
 
• Its capital was Ayodhya, and it was ruled by the famous King Prasenajit during the time of the Buddha.
 
• Kosala was known for its cultural and religious significance and was later annexed by Magadha under King Ajatashatru.
 
 
 
• **Vatsa**
 
 
• Vatsa was located in modern-day Allahabad (Prayagraj) in Uttar Pradesh, with its capital at Kausambi.
 
• The kingdom was known for its trade and commerce and was ruled by King Udayana, a patron of arts and culture.
 
• It played a crucial role in the spread of Buddhism and Jainism.
 
 
 
• **Anga**
 
 
• Anga was situated in the eastern part of India, corresponding to present-day Bihar and Bengal.
 
• Its capital was Champa, which was an important center for trade and commerce.
 
• Anga was annexed by Magadha under the rule of King Bimbisara, contributing to Magadha's expansion.
 
 
 
• **Theme: Mahajanapadas**
 
 
• The Mahajanapadas were 16 powerful and vast kingdoms or oligarchic republics that existed in ancient India during the 6th century BCE.
 
• They were mentioned in ancient Buddhist and Jain texts such as the Anguttara Nikaya and Bhagavati Sutra.
 
• The Mahajanapadas played a critical role in the political, cultural, and economic development of ancient India.
 
• Each Mahajanapada had its own administrative systems, armies, and capitals.

questions.question: In which historical text of India silver coins are mentioned as "rupyarupa"
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Arthashastra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The term "rupyarupa," which refers to silver coins, is mentioned in the **Arthashastra**, an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, economic policy, and military strategy.
 
• The **Arthashastra** was authored by **Kautilya (also known as Chanakya or Vishnugupta)**, a prominent advisor to Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Mauryan Empire.
 
• The text provides detailed insights into the economic system of ancient India, including taxation, trade, and the use of currency such as gold, silver, and copper coins.
 
• "Rupyarupa" specifically refers to silver coins that were used as a medium of exchange in trade and commerce during the Mauryan period.
 
• The Arthashastra is considered one of the earliest and most comprehensive works on governance and economics, reflecting the advanced state of financial systems in ancient India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Upanishads**:

 
 
• The Upanishads are a collection of philosophical texts that form the basis of Hindu spiritual thought and discuss topics like the nature of reality, the self (Atman), and ultimate truth (Brahman).
 
• They do not deal with economic or monetary systems but focus on metaphysical concepts and the pursuit of spiritual knowledge.
 
• Key Upanishads include the Chandogya Upanishad, Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and Katha Upanishad.
 
 
 
• **Puranas**:
 
 
• The Puranas are a genre of ancient Indian literature that primarily consists of myths, legends, and religious teachings.
 
• They describe the stories of deities, creation, cosmology, and the genealogies of gods, sages, and kings.
 
• While some Puranas might touch upon aspects of governance and economy, they do not provide systematic discussions on currency or economic systems like the Arthashastra does.
 
 
 
• **Bhagavad Gita**:
 
 
• The Bhagavad Gita is a 700-verse Hindu scripture that is part of the Indian epic Mahabharata, presenting a dialogue between Lord Krishna and Prince Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra.
 
• It primarily focuses on philosophy, ethics, duty (Dharma), and spiritual practices like devotion (Bhakti), knowledge (Jnana), and disciplined action (Karma).
 
• The text does not contain references to silver coins or economic systems.

questions.question: Who among the following marched to break the salt law in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahatma Gandhi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Mahatma Gandhi led the historic **Dandi March** on 12th March 1930 to protest against the British-imposed salt tax.
 
• The march began from Gandhi's Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad and ended at Dandi, a coastal village in Gujarat, covering approximately **240 miles** over 24 days.
 
• The protest was a key event in the **Civil Disobedience Movement**, symbolizing nonviolent resistance against British colonial rule.
 
• On reaching Dandi on 6th April 1930, Gandhi broke the salt law by making salt from seawater, inspiring millions of Indians to defy the British salt monopoly.
 
• The event drew global attention to India's struggle for independence and demonstrated the power of **Satyagraha (nonviolent resistance).**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lala Lajpat Rai:**

 
 
• Lala Lajpat Rai was a prominent freedom fighter known for his participation in the **Indian Nationalist Movement**.
 
• He played a key role in the formation of the **Punjab National Bank** and contributed to the Swadeshi Movement.
 
• He was famously known as the "**Lion of Punjab**" for his fierce patriotism and leadership.
 
• He led protests against the Simon Commission in 1928, during which he succumbed to injuries inflicted by police lathi-charge.
 
 
 
• **Sarojini Naidu:**
 
 
• Sarojini Naidu, known as the "**Nightingale of India**", was a prominent poet and freedom fighter.
 
• She actively participated in the Civil Disobedience and Quit India Movements and was the first woman to become the **President of the Indian National Congress** in 1925.
 
• Although she did not lead the Dandi March, she was an integral part of Gandhi's Salt Satyagraha and even faced imprisonment for her participation.
 
• Sarojini Naidu later became the **Governor of Uttar Pradesh**, the first woman to hold the position in independent India.
 
 
 
• **Bhagat Singh:**
 
 
• Bhagat Singh was one of India's most renowned revolutionaries who played a pivotal role in the freedom struggle.
 
• He was associated with the **Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA)** and was instrumental in advocating armed resistance against British rule.
 
• Bhagat Singh's actions, such as the assembly bomb incident and the killing of British officer John Saunders, made him a national hero.
 
• Although he did not participate in the Dandi March, his contributions to India's independence were revolutionary and complemented the efforts of nonviolent leaders like Gandhi.

questions.question: Who became the major spokesperson of Muslim league after 1934?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mohammad Ali Jinnah**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Mohammad Ali Jinnah became the primary leader and spokesperson of the All-India Muslim League in 1934.
 
• Jinnah is widely recognized as the key architect of the Pakistan Movement, which ultimately resulted in the partition of British India in 1947.
 
• Under Jinnah’s leadership, the Muslim League transformed into a powerful political organization advocating for the rights of Muslims in India.
 
• He proposed the "Two-Nation Theory," which emphasized the distinct cultural, religious, and political identities of Muslims and Hindus in India.
 
• In 1940, Jinnah presided over the Lahore Resolution, which demanded a separate state for Muslims, later to be known as Pakistan.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad**

 
 
• Maulana Azad was a prominent Indian freedom fighter, scholar, and senior leader of the Indian National Congress.
 
• He actively opposed the partition of India and advocated for Hindu-Muslim unity.
 
• Azad was the first Minister of Education in independent India and played a key role in establishing institutions like IITs and the University Grants Commission (UGC).
 
• He was a recipient of the Bharat Ratna in 1992, posthumously.
 
 
 
• **Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (Badshah Khan)**
 
 
• Known as the "Frontier Gandhi," Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan was a prominent freedom fighter and a staunch follower of Mahatma Gandhi’s non-violent principles.
 
• He founded the Khudai Khidmatgar (Servants of God) movement to oppose British rule in the North-West Frontier Province (now in Pakistan).
 
• Khan was an advocate of Hindu-Muslim unity and opposed the partition of India.
 
• He was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1987, becoming the first non-Indian to receive the honor.
 
 
 
• **The All-India Muslim League**
 
 
• The All-India Muslim League was established in 1906 to promote the political interests of Muslims in British India.
 
• Initially, it aimed to secure Muslim representation in government and protect their rights under British rule.
 
• Over time, under Jinnah’s leadership, the League shifted its focus towards the demand for a separate Muslim state.
 
• The League played a central role in the creation of Pakistan in 1947.

questions.question: Which Varna was at the fourth place among the four known Varnas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Shudra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Varna system in ancient India was a hierarchical division of society into four major groups: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra.
 
• **Shudras** were placed at the fourth and lowest level of the Varna system.
 
• They were primarily tasked with serving the other three Varnas and performing menial or labor-intensive jobs.
 
• Their duties included working as laborers, artisans, and service providers to society, ensuring the smooth functioning of the community.
 
• Unlike the other three Varnas, Shudras were not allowed to study the Vedas or participate in religious rituals traditionally reserved for the upper Varnas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Brahmin**

 
 
• The Brahmins were at the top of the Varna hierarchy and were primarily priests, scholars, and teachers.
 
• They were responsible for performing religious rituals, studying, and teaching the Vedas, and preserving sacred knowledge.
 
• Brahmins enjoyed significant respect and privileges in ancient Indian society.
 
 
 
• **Kshatriya**
 
 
• Kshatriyas were the warrior class and were responsible for protecting the kingdom and its people.
 
• They held positions of power, such as kings, rulers, and military commanders, and were tasked with maintaining law and order.
 
• Their duties included governance, administration, and defense of the land.
 
 
 
• **Vaishya**
 
 
• Vaishyas were the third Varna and were primarily engaged in trade, agriculture, and commerce.
 
• They played a crucial role in the economic development of society by engaging in business and contributing to trade and industry.
 
• Vaishyas were also involved in wealth generation and were allowed to perform certain religious rituals.

questions.concept: Socio - Religious Reform Movements in the 19th and 20th CE India
questions.question: Who was the founder of Satyashodhak Samaj?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jyotirao Phule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Jyotirao Phule** was the founder of the **Satyashodhak Samaj** (Society of Seekers of Truth) in 1873.
 
• The main aim of the Satyashodhak Samaj was to achieve social equality by eradicating caste discrimination and promoting education, especially for the oppressed classes and women.
 
• Phule worked extensively to challenge the dominance of the upper castes and the exploitation of lower castes in the Indian social hierarchy.
 
• He emphasized the importance of education for all, particularly for marginalized communities, and opened schools for girls and lower-caste children.
 
• The organization played a significant role in spreading awareness about social justice and equality in Maharashtra and other parts of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lala Lajpat Rai:**

 
 
• Lala Lajpat Rai was a prominent Indian nationalist, freedom fighter, and social reformer.
 
• He was popularly known as the "Punjab Kesari" (Lion of Punjab).
 
• He played a vital role in the Indian independence movement and was a part of the Lal-Bal-Pal trio, which included Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal.
 
• He is also remembered for leading the protest against the Simon Commission in 1928, during which he sustained injuries that led to his death.
 
 
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi:**
 
 
• Mahatma Gandhi, also known as the "Father of the Nation," was a key leader in India’s struggle for independence from British rule.
 
• He pioneered the philosophy of non-violence (Ahimsa) and civil disobedience as tools for social and political change.
 
• He led several significant movements, including the Dandi March, Quit India Movement, and the Non-Cooperation Movement.
 
• Gandhi’s vision extended to areas such as rural upliftment, self-reliance, and communal harmony.
 
 
 
• **Raja Ram Mohan Roy:**
 
 
• Raja Ram Mohan Roy was a prominent social reformer and the founder of the Brahmo Samaj in 1828.
 
• He is often regarded as the "Father of Modern India" for his contributions to societal transformation during the 19th century.
 
• He campaigned against practices such as Sati and child marriage and advocated for widow remarriage and women’s education.
 
• Raja Ram Mohan Roy also worked to promote modern education and was instrumental in the establishment of the Hindu College in Calcutta (now Kolkata).
 
 
 
• **Satyashodhak Samaj:**
 
 
• The Satyashodhak Samaj was a groundbreaking social reform movement aimed at challenging caste hierarchies and promoting equality.
 
• It worked to empower the oppressed classes, including Dalits and women, through education and awareness.
 
• Jyotirao Phule’s efforts through the Samaj laid the foundation for later movements advocating social justice and caste-based equality in India.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the six major controls of climate of any place?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Human Influence**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Human influence is **not considered one of the six major controls of climate** because the primary factors affecting climate are natural phenomena.
 
• The six major controls of climate include latitude, altitude, pressure and wind systems, distance from the sea, ocean currents, and relief features.
 
• While human activities such as deforestation, urbanization, and emissions do impact the climate, these are categorized as anthropogenic causes and are not part of the natural controls of climate.
 
• Natural climate controls are the physical and geographical factors that determine the climatic characteristics of any region.
 
• The role of human influence is significant in **climate change** rather than being a natural determinant of climate.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Distance from the Sea:**

 
 
• Places near the sea have a moderate climate due to the influence of maritime air masses, whereas inland areas experience extreme climates.
 
• This phenomenon is known as the **continentality effect**.
 
• Proximity to large water bodies helps regulate temperature by absorbing and releasing heat slowly.
 
 
 
• **Latitude:**
 
 
• Latitude plays a crucial role in determining the amount of solar energy received by a region.
 
• Regions near the equator receive more direct sunlight, resulting in higher temperatures, whereas polar areas receive less sunlight and are colder.
 
• This is due to the curvature of the Earth, which affects the angle at which sunlight strikes the surface.
 
 
 
• **Ocean Currents:**
 
 
• Ocean currents significantly influence the climate of coastal regions.
 
• Warm ocean currents, such as the Gulf Stream, raise the temperature of nearby coastal areas, while cold currents, such as the Labrador Current, lower the temperature.
 
• They play a vital role in regulating the global heat balance and affecting weather patterns.

questions.question: Magnetic materials are the materials which _______.

• Magnetic materials are those materials that exhibit magnetism, meaning they can be attracted or repelled by a magnet depending on their magnetic properties.
 
• These materials typically include iron, nickel, cobalt, and their alloys, which are known as ferromagnetic materials.

questions.question: What are the images formed by a plane mirror which could NOT be obtained on a screen called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Virtual**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Images formed by a plane mirror are **virtual**, meaning they cannot be projected onto a screen.
 
• A virtual image is formed when the light rays appear to diverge from a point behind the mirror.
 
• In the case of plane mirrors, virtual images are always of the same size as the object and located at the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.
 
• Virtual images are upright (not inverted) and exhibit lateral inversion, where the left and right sides appear reversed.
 
• Plane mirrors are commonly used in everyday life, such as in bathrooms and dressing rooms, to produce virtual images.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Real Images:**

 
 
• Real images are formed when light rays converge at a point.
 
• They can be projected onto a screen because the light rays physically meet at a specific location.
 
• Real images are inverted relative to the object.
 
• They are typically formed by concave mirrors or converging lenses when the object is placed outside the focal length.
 
 
 
• **Imaginary Images:**
 
 
• The term "imaginary image" is not scientifically valid or used in optics.
 
• It may sometimes be confused with virtual images, but "imaginary" is not a recognized category in the study of image formation.
 
 
 
• **Duplicate Images:**
 
 
• Duplicate images do not refer to any established concept in optics.
 
• It might be used informally to describe identical copies or reflections, but it is not a scientific term related to image formation.
 
 
 
• **Plane Mirror Concept:**
 
 
• Plane mirrors are flat surfaces that reflect light to produce images.
 
• They follow the laws of reflection, where the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
 
• Plane mirrors are widely used in optical devices and everyday applications due to their ability to produce clear, virtual images.

questions.question: Which among the following is NOT an example of capillary action?

options.text: Upward movement of water in a straw
Absorption of ink by blotting pap

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Formation of soap bubbles**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Capillary action** is the ability of a liquid to flow in narrow spaces without the assistance of external forces like gravity.
 
• The formation of soap bubbles does not involve capillary action as it is governed by surface tension and not the movement of liquid through narrow spaces.
 
• In soap bubbles, the surface tension of the soap solution stabilizes the thin layer of liquid, forming a bubble. This process is unrelated to the phenomenon of capillary action.
 
• Capillary action occurs due to the cohesive forces between liquid molecules and adhesive forces between the liquid and solid surfaces, which do not play a role in the formation of soap bubbles.
 
• Examples of capillary action include the upward movement of water in plants, blotting of ink by paper, and water rising in thin tubes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Upward movement of water in a straw:**

 
 
• This is a classic example of capillary action where water rises in a thin straw due to adhesive forces between water molecules and the straw's surface.
 
• Cohesive forces between water molecules also play a role in sustaining the upward movement.
 
• The narrower the straw, the higher the water rises due to the increased role of adhesive forces.
 
 
 
• **Tears moving through the tear duct:**
 
 
• The movement of tears through the tear duct involves capillary action.
 
• The narrow ducts facilitate the flow of liquid (tears) due to the adhesive forces between the tears and the duct walls.
 
• This ensures proper drainage of tears from the eye to the nasal cavity.
 
 
 
• **Absorption of ink by blotting paper:**
 
 
• This phenomenon is another example of capillary action where ink is absorbed into the porous structure of blotting paper.
 
• Adhesive forces between the ink and the paper fibers draw the ink into the small pores of the paper.
 
• This is why blotting paper is specifically designed with a porous structure to enhance capillary action.

questions.question: What is the network of air tubes for gas exchange in insects called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Trachea**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Insects have a specialized respiratory system consisting of a network of air-filled tubes called **tracheae**.
 
• Tracheae are branched, tubular structures that transport oxygen directly to the cells and tissues and remove carbon dioxide.
 
• The tracheae open to the outside through tiny openings called **spiracles** located on the body surface of the insect.
 
• Gas exchange occurs through diffusion, which is facilitated by the thin walls of the tracheoles (fine branches of the trachea).
 
• This system is highly efficient and allows insects to meet their high metabolic demands without the need for a circulatory system to transport oxygen.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Spiracles**

 
 
• Spiracles are external openings on the body of an insect that lead to the tracheal system.
 
• They regulate the entry and exit of gases by opening and closing, which helps prevent water loss.
 
• Spiracles are typically located on the thorax and abdomen and are surrounded by muscles that control their opening and closing.
 
 
 
• **Bronchi**
 
 
• Bronchi are part of the respiratory system in vertebrates, including humans, and not insects.
 
• They are air passages that branch from the trachea into the lungs, where they further divide into smaller bronchioles leading to the alveoli for gas exchange.
 
• This system is different from the direct tracheal system found in insects.
 
 
 
• **Gas Exchange in Insects**
 
 
• Insects rely on passive diffusion for gas exchange, which is why the tracheal system is so efficient for their small body size.
 
• The absence of lungs or a circulatory system for oxygen transport distinguishes their respiratory system from that of vertebrates.
 
• In some aquatic insects, the tracheal system is adapted for underwater breathing using structures like gills or air bubbles.

questions.question: By which process the water evaporates through the stomata present on the surface of the leaves?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Transpiration**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Transpiration** is the process by which water evaporates from the aerial parts of plants, primarily through the stomata on the leaves.
 
• It helps in the **regulation of temperature** in plants and maintains the flow of water and nutrients from the roots to other parts of the plant.
 
• Approximately **90% of water absorbed by plants** is lost through transpiration, indicating its critical role in plant physiology.
 
• Transpiration also creates a suction force called the **transpiration pull**, which helps in the upward movement of water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves.
 
• The rate of transpiration is influenced by environmental factors such as light, temperature, humidity, and wind.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Photosynthesis**

 
 
• Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria convert sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water into glucose and oxygen.
 
• The reaction occurs in the **chloroplasts** of plant cells, containing the green pigment chlorophyll.
 
• This process is essential for producing the food required by plants and indirectly sustains most life on Earth by producing oxygen.
 
• It is represented by the equation: **6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2**.
 
 
 
• **Transportation**
 
 
• Transportation in plants refers to the movement of water, minerals, and nutrients throughout the plant body.
 
• The **xylem** is responsible for transporting water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the rest of the plant, while the **phloem** transports food (sugar) from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
 
• This process is crucial for maintaining plant growth, repair, and reproduction.
 
 
 
• **Evaporation**
 
 
• Evaporation is the process of converting liquid water into water vapor due to heat energy.
 
• Unlike transpiration, evaporation occurs from any exposed surface, such as soil, water bodies, or other non-living surfaces.
 
• It plays a key role in the **water cycle**, helping to transfer moisture from the Earth's surface to the atmosphere.

questions.question: Which among the following is an electronegative element?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fluorine**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Fluorine is the most electronegative element on the periodic table, with an electronegativity value of 3.98 on the Pauling scale.
 
• Electronegativity refers to the ability of an atom to attract electrons in a chemical bond, and fluorine has the strongest ability due to its small atomic size and high effective nuclear charge.
 
• Fluorine is a halogen and belongs to Group 17 of the periodic table, which consists of highly reactive non-metals.
 
• It has seven valence electrons, requiring only one more electron to complete its octet, making it extremely reactive.
 
• Fluorine forms compounds with almost all elements and is widely used in industries such as the production of Teflon, refrigerants, and fluorinated pharmaceuticals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lithium:**

 
 
• Lithium is an alkali metal and belongs to Group 1 of the periodic table.
 
• It has low electronegativity and is highly reactive, particularly with water, to form lithium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
 
• Lithium is commonly used in rechargeable batteries, ceramics, and as a mood-stabilizing drug in psychiatry.
 
 
 
• **Sodium:**
 
 
• Sodium is also an alkali metal from Group 1 and has low electronegativity.
 
• It reacts vigorously with water, forming sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
 
• Sodium compounds, such as sodium chloride (table salt), are essential in human diets and industrial processes.
 
 
 
• **Magnesium:**
 
 
• Magnesium is an alkaline earth metal from Group 2 of the periodic table.
 
• It has moderate electronegativity and is less reactive than alkali metals.
 
• Magnesium is vital for biological systems, especially in chlorophyll for photosynthesis, and is used in alloys, fireworks, and medicines.
 
 
 
• **Electronegativity:**
 
 
• Electronegativity is a measure of an atom's ability to attract bonding electrons.
 
• It increases across a period (from left to right) due to an increase in nuclear charge and decreases down a group due to increased atomic radius and shielding effects.
 
• The periodic trend of electronegativity is essential for predicting the nature of bonds—ionic, covalent, or polar covalent—formed between atoms.

questions.question: In which type of chemical reaction a more reactivetal eplace a less reactive metal?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Displacement Reaction**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Displacement reactions** occur when a more reactive element replaces a less reactive element from its compound.
 
• In the case of metals, a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal in a salt solution. For example, zinc can displace copper from copper sulfate solution because zinc is more reactive than copper.
 
• The reactivity of metals is determined by their position in the **reactivity series**. Metals higher in the series are more reactive and can displace metals lower in the series.
 
• Displacement reactions are widely used in industries, such as extraction of metals from their ores (e.g., iron from iron oxide using carbon).
 
• This type of reaction is also observed in halogens (non-metals) where a more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from its compound.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Neutralization Reaction:**

 
 
• A neutralization reaction occurs when an acid reacts with a base to form salt and water.
 
• The reaction can be represented as: **Acid + Base → Salt + Water**.
 
• Example: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) reacts with sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to form sodium chloride (NaCl) and water.
 
• These reactions are commonly used to control pH levels in various applications such as agriculture and wastewater treatment.
 
 
 
• **Decomposition Reaction:**
 
 
• Decomposition reactions involve the breakdown of a single compound into two or more simpler substances.
 
• These reactions are often triggered by heat, light, or electricity.
 
• Example: Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) decomposes to calcium oxide (CaO) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) upon heating.
 
• They are widely used in processes like cement manufacturing and the extraction of metals.
 
 
 
• **Redox Reaction:**
 
 
• Redox reactions are chemical reactions that involve the transfer of electrons between two substances.
 
• Oxidation refers to the loss of electrons, while reduction refers to the gain of electrons.
 
• Example: In the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form water, hydrogen is oxidized, and oxygen is reduced.
 
• These reactions are fundamental to processes such as combustion, corrosion, and cellular respiration.

questions.question: Polythene and PVC are some of the examples of ____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Thermoplastics**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Thermoplastics** are a type of plastic that becomes soft when heated and hardens upon cooling. This process can be repeated multiple times without significant degradation.
 
• Polythene (polyethylene) and PVC (polyvinyl chloride) are examples of thermoplastics.
 
• Thermoplastics are known for their flexibility, lightweight nature, and ability to be reshaped or remolded.
 
• They are widely used in industries for making packaging materials, pipes, bottles, toys, and various household items.
 
• Unlike thermosetting plastics, thermoplastics do not undergo a permanent chemical change when heated, allowing them to be recycled easily.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Thermosetting Plastics:**

 
 
• These plastics harden permanently after being molded once and cannot be remolded or reheated.
 
• Examples include Bakelite and melamine. These are used in applications such as electrical switches, handles of utensils, and laminates.
 
• Unlike thermoplastics, thermosetting plastics undergo a chemical change during the curing process, making them rigid and heat-resistant.
 
 
 
• **Acrylic:**
 
 
• Acrylic is a synthetic polymer material known for its transparency, strength, and lightweight nature.
 
• It is commonly used as a glass substitute in products like aquariums, lenses, and display cases.
 
• Acrylic is not categorized as a thermoplastic or thermosetting plastic but is a unique polymer with distinct properties.
 
 
 
• **Plastics:**
 
 
• Plastics are synthetic materials made from polymers that can be molded into various shapes and forms.
 
• They are broadly classified into two categories: thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics, based on their behavior when exposed to heat.
 
• Plastics are widely used in industries, from packaging and construction to electronics and automotive manufacturing, due to their versatility.

questions.question: Which chemical is used in refrigerators, air conditioners (AC) and aerosol sprays that form air pollutants?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chlorofluorocarbon**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are synthetic compounds composed of carbon, chlorine, and fluorine.
 
• CFCs are widely used in refrigerators, air conditioners (ACs), and aerosol sprays as refrigerants and propellants due to their chemical stability and non-flammability.
 
• However, CFCs are a major contributor to air pollution as they cause the depletion of the ozone layer when released into the atmosphere.
 
• When CFCs reach the stratosphere, they release chlorine atoms under ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which then reacts with ozone (O3), breaking it down into oxygen molecules (O2).
 
• The Montreal Protocol (1987) was established to phase out the production and use of ozone-depleting substances, including CFCs, to protect the ozone layer.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sulphur dioxide (SO2):**

questions.question: What is the tendency of biological systems to resist change in internal environment called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Homeostasis**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Homeostasis** refers to the ability of biological systems to maintain a stable internal environment despite changes in external conditions.
 
• It is essential for the survival of living organisms, ensuring optimal functioning of cells, organs, and systems.
 
• Examples of homeostasis include temperature regulation, pH balance, and the maintenance of blood glucose levels.
 
• Mechanisms like negative feedback loops play a critical role in maintaining homeostasis; for instance, sweating to cool the body when it overheats.
 
• Disruption in homeostasis can lead to diseases or dysfunction, such as diabetes caused by an inability to regulate blood sugar levels.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Isobarism**

 
 
• Isobarism refers to the phenomenon where different chemical elements have the same atomic mass but differ in atomic number.
 
• For example, carbon-14 and nitrogen-14 are isobars.
 
• This concept is related to nuclear physics and chemistry and does not pertain to biological systems.
 
 
 
• **Ammensalism**
 
 
• Ammensalism is a type of biological interaction where one organism is harmed while the other remains unaffected.
 
• An example is the production of antibiotics by fungi, which can inhibit bacterial growth without benefiting the fungi.
 
• This concept explains ecological relationships and is unrelated to the regulation of internal environments.
 
 
 
• **Symbiosis**
 
 
• Symbiosis is a biological relationship between two organisms where at least one benefits from the interaction.
 
• It includes mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, the other is unaffected), and parasitism (one benefits, the other is harmed).
 
• Though symbiosis is crucial in ecosystems, it does not explain the regulation of internal conditions within organisms.

questions.question: Which place is the first in the world to be served by drones for commercial delivery?

options.text: New York, United States of America

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Reykjavik, Iceland**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Reykjavik, Iceland, became the first city globally to implement drones for commercial delivery services in 2017.
 
• This pioneering initiative was led by Flytrex, an Israeli drone logistics company, in collaboration with Icelandic retailer AHA.
 
• Drone deliveries in Reykjavik focused on transporting food, groceries, and small goods, significantly reducing delivery times by up to 60% compared to traditional methods.
 
• The drones operated on pre-programmed routes, ensuring efficient, safe, and fast transport across urban and sparsely populated areas.
 
• The unique geography of Iceland, characterized by remote regions and challenging terrain, made it an ideal testing ground for drone-based delivery systems.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **New York, United States of America**

 
 
• New York is a global hub for technology and innovation, but it was not the first city to adopt drones for commercial delivery.
 
• Drone delivery services in the U.S. are being developed and tested by companies like Amazon and UPS, with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulating drone operations.
 
• Companies are primarily focused on implementing drone deliveries for medical supplies and retail goods in rural and suburban areas.
 
 
 
• **Delhi, India**
 
 
• India has been exploring drone technology for various applications, including agricultural monitoring, disaster management, and medical supply delivery.
 
• In recent years, drone delivery pilots have been conducted, particularly in rural areas, to transport vaccines and essential goods.
 
• However, Delhi has not been the first city to implement drones for commercial delivery services.
 
 
 
• **Copenhagen, Denmark**
 
 
• Copenhagen is known for its technological advancements and smart city initiatives.
 
• Denmark has been leveraging drones for purposes like medical supply transport and environmental monitoring rather than commercial delivery services.
 
• Although Denmark is investing in drone technology, Reykjavik, Iceland, holds the distinction of being the first city to implement drones for commercial deliveries.
 
 
 
• **Drone Technology and Commercial Deliveries**
 
 
• Drones are unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) equipped with advanced sensors and navigation systems for various applications.
 
• In commercial delivery, drones are used to transport goods such as food, medical supplies, and packages over short distances.
 
• Drone deliveries offer faster transportation, reduced operational costs, and accessibility to remote areas.
 
• Regulations, safety concerns, and technological challenges remain key barriers to the widespread adoption of drone logistics worldwide.

questions.question: The “question hour” in the Parliament ensures ________.
questions.solution:
**The correct option is ' Executive accountability towards the legislature'. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

 
• **Question Hour **is an important feature of the parliamentary system of government.
 
• It is held in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
 
• During the Question Hour, Members of Parliament can ask questions to the Ministers regarding the administration of their respective ministries.
 
• **This allows the MPs to hold the Executive accountable for their actions and policies.**
 
• **The questions can be broadly classified into three categories:**
 
• **Starred Questions**:
 
 
• These are the questions which require an oral answer from the Minister on the floor of the House.
 
• The member who asks the question is given an opportunity to ask a supplementary question.
 
 
 
• **Unstarred Questions:**
 
 
• These are the questions which do not require an oral answer.
 
• The written answer is given by the Minister to the House.
 
 
 
• **Short Notice Questions:**
 
 
• These are the questions which are asked on an urgent matter.
 
• The member is required to give a notice of less than 10 days to the Minister.
